title: The Two Harvests of Christ
english: At that same evening they were performing rites, for even salvations—I say of both the living and the dead—were being enacted. The Jew was binding a lamb for slaughter, while the Gentile was worshipping God in the flesh. One was looking at a shadow, while the other ran to God as the sun. Those who had bound Christ were departing, while the Gentiles were welcoming him willingly. Some offered animal sacrifices, but others offered a God-body sacrifice.

The Jews remembered the crossing out of Egypt, but the Gentiles proclaimed the redemption from error. And where are these things? In Zion, the city of the Great King, in which salvation worked in the midst of the earth. In the midst of two living beings, Jesus the God-child was made known; in the midst of Father and Spirit, the two living beings, life from life, he says, being known as life, and being born in a manger in the midst of angels and men. He lies as a cornerstone in the midst of two peoples; he is preached in the midst of Law and Prophets together; he is seen on the mountain in the midst of Moses and Elijah; he is known to the good-hearted thief in the midst of the two thieves; he sits as eternal judge in the midst of the present life and the life to come; and in the midst of living and dead today, having made a double life and salvation.

Again I say, a double life: a double birth, namely both birth and rebirth. Listen to the matters of Christ's double offspring, and marvel at the wonders. An angel announced to Mary, the mother of Christ, the birth; but an angel announced to Mary Magdalene the fearful rebirth from the tomb. At night Christ is born in Bethlehem; again at night he is reborn in Zion. Swaddling clothes are received for the birth; swaddling clothes are also wrapped here. Having been born receiving myrrh, he received myrrh in the tomb, and aloes are received.

There, Joseph, the virile man, was the husband of Mary; but here, Joseph of Arimathea is shown as the undertaker of our life. In Bethlehem and in a manger is the place; but even in the tomb, the place is as if a manger. First of all, shepherds were evangelizing the birth of Christ; but also, first of all, shepherds were evangelized of the rebirth of Christ from the dead. There, the angel cried 'Rejoice!' to the Virgin; and here, 'Rejoice!' to the...

Christ, the messenger of a great will, has cried out to the women. In the first generation, Christ entered earthly Jerusalem after forty days and approached God, offering as a firstborn pair of grapes. But also, in the resurrection from the dead, Christ ascended to the upper Jerusalem after forty days, from where he did not depart, and into the true Holy of Holies as an incorruptible firstborn from the dead; there he offered to God and Father as two spotless grapes, our soul and our flesh. He was received, like a Simeon, by the God and Father of old, in unwritten embraces within his own bosom.

If you hear these things only as a myth and not with faith, the unbroken seals of the memory of Christ's rebirth accuse you. For just as Christ was born from a Virgin, even though the locks of the all-conceived womb of the virginal nature were sealed, so the rebirth of Christ has been accomplished while the seals of the tomb remained unopened. Let us hear the sacred words concerning how, when, and by whom the Life, Christ, is laid in a tomb.

It is said that when evening came, a man named Joseph, rich in name, arrived. This man dared to go to Pilate and requested from him the body of Jesus. A mortal went to a mortal, asking to take God; he asks for the God of mortals; clay asks to take the Maker of all; the chaff asks of the chaff to take the heavenly fire; the wretched drop asks of the wretched drop to take the abyss. Who has seen this? Who has ever heard this? A man is granted the Creator of men by a man; the lawless submits to being granted the boundary and the law by the lawless; the unjudging judge allows the Judge of judges to be released into a tomb.

It is said that when evening came, a man named Joseph, rich in name, arrived. He was truly rich, having brought the whole composite subsistence of the Lord. He was truly rich, because he received the dual essence of Christ from Pilate. And indeed he was rich, because he was worthy to take the priceless pearl. He was rich, for he carried a purse that was a vessel of the treasure of divinity. For how could he not be rich, having acquired the life and salvation of the world? And how could he not be rich...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Homilia in divini corporis sepulturam u01-rem-early

title: The Stranger and the Dead God
english: Did Joseph receive the gift of the One who nourishes and rules all things? When darkness fell, it was because the sun of righteousness had been left in Hades. Consequently, a man named Joseph, wealthy in reputation, came from Arimathea, remaining in hiding due to the fear of the Jews. Nicodemus also came, he who had approached Jesus by night. This is a mystery of mysteries, a hidden thing. Two secret disciples come to conceal Jesus in a tomb, teaching through their own concealment the hidden mystery in Hades of the God hidden in the flesh.

One exceeds the other in his disposition toward Christ. For Nicodemus was magnanimous in myrrh and in flame, but Joseph is worthy of praise for his boldness and confidence toward Pilate. This man, having cast away all fear, dared to enter before Pilate to request the body of Jesus; and having entered, he used words with great wisdom so that he might reach his desired goal. He did not use any entanglements or lofty words with Pilate, lest he should provoke this man to anger and fail in his request. He does not say to him: Give me the body of Jesus, who a short time ago darkened the sun, cast down the stones, shook the earth, opened the tombs, and tore the temple veil. He says nothing of such magnitude to Pilate.

Instead, he asks for something pitiful, and something small in the eyes of all. O judge, I have come to ask of you a very small request. He says: Give me a corpse for burial: the body of that Jesus of Nazareth, judged by you—the poor Jesus, the homeless Jesus, the crucified Jesus, the naked, the insignificant Jesus, the carpenter's son, the prisoner, the outcast, the stranger, the unknown one through alienation, the well-disposed, and the one hung upon all. Give me this stranger; for what does the body of this stranger profit you? Give me this stranger; for he came from far from this land to save the stranger, for he descended into the darkness to carry the stranger up. Give me this stranger; for he himself also exists as a stranger. Give me this stranger, whose land we strangers do not know. Give me this stranger, whose father we strangers do not know. Give me this stranger, whose place, lineage, and manner we strangers do not know.

The stranger. Give to me this stranger, who lived a life and an existence as a stranger among strangers. Give to me this Nazarene stranger, whose birth and manner we strangers do not know. Give to me this voluntary stranger, who has no place here to bow his head. Give to me this stranger, who as a stranger was born upon a manger, and from that same manger fled as a stranger from Herod. Give to me this stranger, who was made a stranger among the stalks in Egypt, possessing no city, no village, no house, no dwelling, and no relatives; for this stranger happens to be in a foreign land.

Give to me, O leader, this one naked upon a tree, so that I may cover the one who covered my own nature with nakedness. Give to me this dead one who is also God, so that I may cover the one who covered my own lawlessness. Give to me, O leader, a dead man, the one who buried my own sin by the Jordan. I plead for a dead man who was wronged by all, sold by a friend, betrayed by a disciple, persecuted by brothers, and struck by a slave. I advocate for a dead man, the one condemned by those whom he freed from slavery, the one made to drink the vinegar by them, the one wounded by those whom he healed, the one abandoned by the disciples, and the one deprived of his own mother. I cry out for a dead man, O leader, the one hung upon a tree without a home. For there is not present for this one a father on earth, nor a friend, nor a disciple, nor a relative, nor a burial provider; but he is alone, the only-begotten of the only, God in the world, and no other.

These things having been thus said by Joseph to Pilate, Pilate commanded that the all-holy body of Jesus be given to him. And having come to the place of Golgotha, he took down God in flesh from the tree, and places him upon the earth: God in flesh naked, and not a mere man. And he is seen lying below, the one who drew all things up above; and briefly he becomes breath, the life and breath of all; and he is seen bodiless, the one who created the many-bodied; and he lies face down, the resurrection of all; and God dies in the flesh, the one who raises the dead; and briefly the thunder of the Word of God is silent; and the dragon who holds the earth is lifted up of old. For indeed, or perhaps, O Joseph, having asked and having received, do you know whom you have taken? Or perhaps, having approached...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Homilia in divini corporis sepulturam u01-rem-mid

title: The Paradox of the Incarnation and the Burial
english: By the cross, in lowering Jesus, do you know whom you have borne? If you truly know whom you hold, you have now become rich. How then do you perform such a terrifying care for this God-body of Jesus? Your desire is praiseworthy, but your manner is even more praiseworthy.

For do you not tremble, carrying upon hands him whom the cherubim tremble at? With what fear do you strip the soft flesh of that divine body? How do you reverently restrain your eye, not staring and uncovering the nature of the flesh of God, who is beyond nature? Tell me, Joseph, do you bury a corpse toward the east, even the Sunrise of sunrises? Do you close with your death-like fingers the eyes of him whom the spotless finger opened for the blind? Do you close the mouth of him whom the mouth-opener opened? Do you withdraw the hands of him who stretched out the dried-up hands? Do you bind the feet in a death-like way, him who gave walking feet to the motionless? Do you lift upon a bed him who commanded the paralytic to lift his bed and walk?

Do you offer myrrh to him who emptied himself with heavenly myrrh and sanctified the world? Do you dare to shame the side of the God-body of Jesus, still bleeding, who is the God who healed the bleeding woman? Do you wash the body of God with water, he who washed everyone and gave cleansing? What lamps will you light for the true Light who enlightened every man? What funeral songs will you sing to him who is silently praised by every heavenly host? Do you weep for him as a dead man, he who wept for Lazarus the four-day dead? Do you make laments for him who gives joy to all and dissolved the sorrow of Eve?

Yet I bless your hands, O Joseph, having served and having touched even the bleeding God-body hands and feet of Jesus. I bless your hands having approached the bleeding side of God, before Thomas, the faithful-unfaithful and praised curious one. I bless your mouth having been filled without greed and having been united to the mouth of Jesus, and having been filled from there with the Holy Spirit. I bless...

Having set your eyes to the eyes of Jesus and received the true light from there, I bless you whose face approached the face of God. I bless you whose shoulders bore Him who bears all; I bless you whose head approached the head of all, Jesus; I bless you whose hands bore Him who bears all. I bless Joseph and Nicodemus. For they have become gods before the cherubim, having exalted and carried Him within themselves. They have become ministers before the six-winged God, not with wings, but covering the Lord with veils and honoring Him.

Whom the cherubim tremble at, this one Joseph and Nicodemus carry upon their shoulders, and all the ranks of the incorporeal stand forth. For Joseph and Nicodemus came; surely all ran together, even the God-sent of the angels. The cherubim anticipate, the seraphim run together, and the thrones assist in carrying, covering the six wings. The many-eyed ones shake, seeing Jesus the incorporeal in the flesh, and the powers cover Him. The principalities sing, the ranks shake, and all the armies of the transformed ranks stand forth. Being amazed at themselves, they run about, saying: 'What is this fearful word, and dread, and trembling, and awe? What is this great, and paradoxical, and incomprehensible sight?' He who is above us, to us the incorporeal, is as God naked and invisible; but below, to mortals, He is naked and visible.

How Joseph and Nicodemus care for Him with unconcern, while the cherubim stand by with reverence. When did He who does not leave the above descend? How did He who is within go out? How did He who fills all come upon the earth? How did He who eludes all depart? He who is above with the Father as God without ceasing, is below with the mother as a mortal truly without ceasing. He who was never revealed to us, how does He appear to men as God, both human and man-loving? How was the invisible seen? How was the bodiless incarnated? How did the impassible suffer? How did the judge stand at the judgment seat? How did life taste death? How is the uncontainable contained in a tomb? How does He who does not leave the bosom of the Father dwell in a tomb? How does He enter the gate of a cave, having opened the gate of Paradise, but not having breached the gates of the Virgin, but the gates of...
